title: One-clean-qubit spectroscopy of simulated Kitaev chains
abstract: Spin qubits in gate-defined quantum dots provide a highly programmable platform for simulating condensed-matter phenomena. In this work, we introduce a digital-analog quantum simulation protocol for extracting the single-particle spectrum of a Kitaev chain. The Kitaev chain is mapped onto qubits via the standard Jordan-Wigner transformation and implemented as a drive-engineered, $N$-site transverse-field Ising model (TFIM) in a linear array of quantum dots. We show that periodically toggling the analog-simulation parameters conditioned on the state of a control qubit causes the dynamics of this control qubit to stroboscopically match the output of the one-clean-qubit (DQC1) model of computation, thereby yielding the full spectrum of the TFIM from measurements of a single spin. Classical postprocessing can then be used to isolate the $N$ single-particle energies of the Kitaev chain from the $2^N$ eigenenergies of the TFIM. By varying the strength of the Rabi drive used to engineer the synthetic transverse field, the spectral signature of the crossover from the trivial to the topological regime of the Kitaev chain could then be mapped out with measurements of just one spin.
summary: This paper proposes a novel quantum simulation protocol to measure the single-particle spectrum of a Kitaev chain using only measurements on one spin qubit. By mapping the chain to a TFIM on quantum dots, the authors use controlled quantum gates to stroboscopically extract the full spectrum from the control qubit's coherence. This technique is significant because it allows probing topological phase transitions in solid-state systems with minimal measurement overhead.
main_problem: The primary goal is to extract the single-particle energy spectrum of a Kitaev chain using measurements performed on only one physical spin qubit.
main_result: The authors demonstrate a digital-analog quantum simulation protocol that achieves this by stroboscopically matching the system's dynamics to the output of a one-clean-qubit computation model.
method: The method involves mapping the Kitaev chain to a transverse-field Ising model (TFIM) implemented on spin qubits in quantum dots, and then using controlled-Y gates conditioned on a control qubit to extract spectral information.
model_or_system: The system uses spin qubits in gate-defined quantum dots arranged in a $2 	imes N$ array. The physics is modeled by the Kitaev chain, which is realized via a drive-engineered, $N$-site TFIM Hamiltonian, $H_{	ext{TFIM}}$.
key_observables: The coherence of the control qubit ($\langle\sigma_+angle_t$) is the key observable used to map out the full spectrum, particularly the signature of the crossover between trivial and topological regimes.
important_parameters: The ratio of coupling strengths ($J$ vs $h$) controls the phase of the Kitaev chain, with the transition occurring at $J=h$. The Rabi drive strength controls the synthetic transverse field.
main_assumptions: The protocol assumes the ability to periodically toggle analog-simulation parameters and relies on classical postprocessing to isolate the desired single-particle energies from the full TFIM eigenenergies.

paper_structure: The paper introduces the physical platform and the problem (Kitaev spectroscopy). It details the digital-analog simulation protocol, showing how the TFIM evolution is mapped onto a controlled qubit dynamics. Finally, it discusses the extraction of the single-particle spectrum from the measured single-spin coherence.
why_interesting: This work provides a concrete, near-term experimental pathway to probe fundamental topological phases (like those described by the Kitaev chain) using only local measurements, which is highly relevant for quantum simulation in solid-state systems.
